I've got a milp model could never run an optimal result for a limited time on my laptop.
I set a time_limit parameter for it to get a sub-optimal solution, and found that when it runs longer than 3000 seconds , jupyter notebook seemed down and the fan for cpu stoped buzzing too. 
Althought  the code-block in the jupyter notebook shown it would be still "running" , no matter how long I wait for it , it never stop again until I stop the python kernel.

### Describe your issue.

The HiGHS linear optimization software implementation in the `milp` function claims having found an optimal solution but always returns an infeasible one for the following 8 variables, 6 equality constraints integer linear program. I obtained the correct solution (which is not that far off) through GLPK's solver.

Looks similar to #22812.

]

title: BUG: filter out unhelpful & noisy numpy warnings in implementation, not in tests
body:
This was surfaced by #19804, causing me to take a look where those warnings were coming from. I was surprised that - in the example below at least - the warnings are duplicated between scipy & numpy (not caught by the new pytest 8 because the messages are identical).

Looking [closer](https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Ascipy%2Fscipy+%2FMean+of+empty+slice%5C.%7Cinvalid+value+encountered%2F&type=code), we're filtering out a lot of warnings in tests that should IMO really be filtered out in the implementations, rather than the tests.

As an example:
```
>>> from scipy import stats
>>> stats.skew([])
[...]/scipy/stats/_stats_py.py:1175: RuntimeWarning: Mean of empty slice.
  mean = a.mean(axis, keepdims=True)
[...]/numpy/core/_methods.py:121: RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in divide
  ret = um.true_divide(
[...]/numpy/core/fromnumeric.py:3504: RuntimeWarning: Mean of empty slice.
  return _methods._mean(a, axis=axis, dtype=dtype,
[...]/numpy/core/_methods.py:129: RuntimeWarning: invalid value encountered in scalar divide
  ret = ret.dtype.type(ret / rcount)
nan
```

4 warnings here are at least 3 too many, and we need to filter at least the ones from numpy; though IMO even "Mean of empty slice" is not helpful, and we could perhaps just return `np.nan` without a warning.

title: DOC: 1.17 API changes not mentioned in the 1.17.0rc1 release notes
body:
I already pinged @tylerjereddy for a couple of these, but I thought it could help to have an overview of all them, so here goes:

- https://github.com/scipy/scipy-stubs/pull/1035
	- ~`integrate.lsoda`: `nsteps` constructor parameter default changed from 500 to 5000~
	- `integrate`: The `BDF`, `DOP853`, `RK23`, `RK45`, `OdeSolver`, `DenseOutput`, `ode`, and `complex_ode` classes now support subscription, making them [generic types](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-generic-type) , for compatibility with [scipy-stubs](https://github.com/scipy/scipy-stubs). See https://github.com/scipy/scipy-stubs/#scipyintegrate for their generic type signatures.
- https://github.com/scipy/scipy-stubs/pull/1037
	- `interpolate`: The `AAA`, `*Interpolator`, `*Poly`, and `*Spline` classes now support subscription, making them [generic types](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-generic-type) , for compatibility with [scipy-stubs](https://github.com/scipy/scipy-stubs). See https://github.com/scipy/scipy-stubs/#scipyinterpolate for their generic type signatures.
	- `interpolate.AAA`: Like `FloaterHormannInterpolator`, `AAA` also gained a new `axis` parameter
	- `interpolate.generate_knots`: Like `make_splrep` and `make_splprep`, `generate_knots` also gained a new `bc_type` keyword-only parameter.
	- `intepolate.NdBSpline`: The (mutable) instance attribute `.c` was changed into a (read-only) `@property`.
	- `intepolate.RegularGridInterpolator`: The (mutable) instance attributes `.grid` and `.values` were changed into (read-only) properties.
- https://github.com/scipy/scipy-stubs/pull/1041
	- `optimize`: The `BroydenFirst`, `*Jacobian`, and `Bounds` classes now support subscription, making them [generic types](https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-generic-type) , for compatibility with [scipy-stubs](https://github.com/scipy/scipy-stubs). title: TST: stats.rv_continuous: standards for distribution-specific tests
body:
`test_continuous_basic` does a reasonably complete job of testing the relationship between a continuous distribution's `pdf` method and its other methods using probability distribution identities. It may have blind spots (e.g. if the parameters defined in `_distn_params` do not exercise all code paths) and some tests aren't very sensitive (e.g. generic RVS test), but typically we can rely on these "generic tests" in `test_continuous_basic` to find inconsistencies between methods. (Let's discuss deficiencies in the generic tests in gh-15928, not here.)

Of course, the generic tests can't detect whether the distribution class represents the _intended_ distribution. For this reason, we need (at a minimum) one "distribution-specific" test. That is, one method of each distribution (usually the PDF) must be tested against reference values, such as those from published tables, other software (e.g. Mathematica, R), or some other _sufficiently independent_ implementation of the method being tested (e.g. a naive implementation that is easily compared against reference formulas, or even using another SciPy distribution that _is_ tested against a reference).

There are times when we want to go beyond generic tests and the minimum distribution-specific tests. For example, when we override distribution methods to avoid numerical difficulties, we will often add tests to show that the implementation actually avoids those numerical difficulties. Reference values for these tests may come from published tables, other software (provided that it is believed to avoid the numerical difficulties in question), or from a naive implementation using `mpmath` (with high `dps`). Another example of when we might want to add distribution-specific tests is when the generic tests are too slow (e.g. included in `test_continuous_basic.distxslow`).

However, there may be cases in which we go beyond the generic tests and the minimum distribution-specific tests when we don't need to. Adding unnecessary tests may not actually improve the strength of the test suite, but it may increase author time, reviewer time, and test suite time. Another problem is that unnecessary tests may add a _false_ sense of security.

The purpose of this issue is to try to reach a consensus on what tests are necessary, what are acceptable, and what should be avoided. I don't mean that we need to purge the existing test suite of unnecessary tests, but I'd like to identify what we'd like to see in the future. 

Let's start with a recent conversation as an example
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/17794#issuecomment-1386054932

Should it be _required_ to add a distribution-specific test of the CDF method if there is already a sufficient test of the PDF method? 
Is it acceptable to include one if the author is willing? 
Or should it be omitted?

(I think that the fact that this implementation loses accuracy in the tails is a separate issue. Yes, it would have been preferable if there were tests during development of the distribution to expose the problem, and it would be great if the implementation had avoided the problem. In this case, we would certainly want to have distribution-specific test of the CDF in the tails, and we'll want to add those tests when gh-17805 is resolved, but are they needed now as part of gh-17794?)

title: BUG: zeta(1/2, 1) returns nan
body:
### Describe your issue.

The Hurwitz zeta function at 1/2, 1 is equivalent to Riemann zeta function at 1/2 and so `zeta(1/2, 1) = zeta(1/2) = -1.46...` (See [WolframAlpha](https://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=zeta%281%2F2%29)) but [`scipy.special.zeta`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.special.zeta.html) returns `nan`. This may be expected behavior but if so it would be nice to have documentation for this behavior.

Related issue: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/68110

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
from scipy.special import zeta

# correct
output = zeta(1 / 2)
print(output)

# wrong
output = zeta(1 / 2, 1)
print(output)
```

nan

title: ENH: linalg: close performance gaps vs `np.linalg`
body:
## Brief 
When investigating an issue related to the potential parallelization of the `eig`/`eigh` family of function, simulations have suggested that when comparing the `linalg` modules of `numpy` and `scipy`, the former is in almost all occassions faster for smaller arrays. When using larger arrays this performance difference is partially amortized, but for some functions the issue remains.

## Related work
In #23673 it was reported that there is a difference in how `numpy` and `scipy` allow for parallelization of the `eig`/`eigh` family of functions. The latest hypothesis, which appears to be confirmed when comparing the `standard` to `free-threaded` implementations of `python`, is that this might be related to the handling of the `global interpreter lock` (`GIL`) by both modules.

## Investigations
When diving deeper into the codebases of both packages, it was found that neither of them appears to explicitly release the `GIL` at first sight. Furthermore, `numpy` even explicitly uses another lock prior to calling into `LAPACK` functions. 

To see if  `numpy` did not release the `GIL` somewhere else, a simulation was set up in which a set of functions that are present in both the `numpy` and `scipy` `linalg` modules are tested against each other, both in a "standard looping" fashion as well as in an attempt to parallelize them using `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor`. 

The setup of the first experiment is the following:
- Arrays of size \[513 x 20 x 20\], which can be considered to be quite relevant for typical signal processing applications in the frequency domain. If a right-hand side for an equation is needed, this is provided as a \[513 x 20 x 1\] array.
- Making use of the `timeit.timeit` function, measure the execution times for 1000 calls to each function of the following script: [linalg_comparison.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22908990/linalg_comparison.py)

The results of this benchmark for different versions of the python interpreter are detailed below. All python interpreters were downloaded from `python-build-standalone` using `uv`. All experiments used the following package versions: `numpy == 2.3.3` and `scipy == 1.16.2` (installed using `uv` from `pip`). All execution times are in seconds.

## Preliminary conclusions
These results suggest a few notable things:
- Perhaps one of the most important conclusions of these experiments is that the fact that `numpy` can be used for parallelization of the `eig` family of functions appears to be more of a coincidence than a real trend. The other functions in this test suite suffer from the same problem as mentioned in #23673 , namely that they get slower when trying to exploit thread-level parallelism. This is, however, out of scope for this issue: it appears to be more of an inconsistency on the `numpy` side. It could be worth investigating whether thread-level parallelism might be enabled in the `scipy.linalg` module without requiring to use the `free-threaded` version of python, but this would require its own issue.
- The main reason for opening this issue is that, at least for this specific size of matrices, there appear to be some big discrepancies in terms of the execution times. In pretty much every ran benchmark, the `scipy` version was considerably slower than the `numpy` equivalent, although there are a few, small, exceptions. The most notable one being the `solve` function where `scipy` is approximately 4x slower than `numpy`. 

## Further investigations
In order to validate whether this issue could be related to the `transient response` of the function handling, i.e. if `scipy` is a bit less efficient in handing of the functions to the `LAPACK` driver, the experiments were repeated for python 3.13 using slightly bigger arrays of size \[513 x 50 x 50\] and \[513 x 50 x 1\] respectively.

## Conclusions
This suggests that using larger arrays might indeed help out in amortizing this additional overhead caused by `scipy`. However, as mentioned before, the smaller arrays used earlier on are also quite likely to be encountered in typical workloads. 

Perhaps more importantly, it also appears as if the issue with `solve`, and by extension `lstsq` being significantly slower in `scipy` is not resolved by going to these larger arrays.

title: BUG: optimize: `minimize(... method='BFGS')` float32 behaviour is not consistent
body:
### Describe your issue.

Hi, 

While investigating poor BFGS convergence, 
I noticed that the behaviour of BFGS in particular with 32-bit inputs is I believe not correct. 
Specifically, here's an example of a Rosenbrock function with analytical gradient that fails to converge.

I have investigated this https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/19024 issue, but I think that analysis of the 
_minimize_bfgs  with the 32-bit input vector inputs there is not accurate. 
In fact this 
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/484575582f6e4c2f84e7de1f5625a11a072ba50b/scipy/optimize/_optimize.py#L1440 line will introduce the 'pk' to be float64 in the very first iteration even if all the function values and gradients are 32-bit. The reason for this is np.dot product of int and float32 gives float64

```
In [3]: np.dot(np.ones((2,2),dtype=int),np.ones(2,dtype=np.float32)).dtype
Out[3]: dtype('float64')

```
Because of this, all the further code down the line will have deal with a weird mixture of float32/float64s.  

In fact even if I change the input vector x0 in my test to be float64 x0, bfgs still fails to converge to [1,1]. However if I change a single line here 

https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/484575582f6e4c2f84e7de1f5625a11a072ba50b/scipy/optimize/_optimize.py#L1440 to 

```
        pk = -np.dot(Hk, gfk).astype(gfk.dtype)
```
After that change the code converges. 

To be honest, I don't think this is the only change needed to make the 32-bit more behaviour correct, because even after this change the purely 32 -bit code does not converge, and one of the reason is the usage of amin/amax of 1e-100/1e100 which immediately overflow/underflow, leading to this kind of warnings:

```
/home/skoposov/pyenv_dir/pyenv312/lib/python3.12/site-packages/scipy/optimize/_dcsrch.py:324: RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in cast
  if stp > self.stpmax:
[3.9961147e+00 2.1209834e+04] 4.4917993e+10
/home/skoposov/pyenv_dir/pyenv312/lib/python3.12/site-packages/scipy/optimize/_dcsrch.py:385: RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in cast
  if stp == self.stpmax and f <= ftest and g <= self.gtest:

```

If I change the amin/amax and  change the line
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/484575582f6e4c2f84e7de1f5625a11a072ba50b/scipy/optimize/_optimize.py#L1428
to 
```
    I = np.eye(N, dtype=gfk.dtype)
```
then I can see all at least all the variables throughout minimize_bfgs are staying as float32, but the code still does not converge. From investigating that I think this okay, as bfgs hits the point of constant function value due to 32-bitness. 


Summarizing, I think the existing code should at least not use the int type for I matrix, and not use amax/amin that overflow/underflow with 32-bits. Alternatively, all the linear search have to be done in 64-bit.

Thanks, 
  Sergey 

### Reproducing Code Example

```python
import numpy as np
# import _optimize
import scipy.optimize._optimize as _optimize


def rosenbrock(x):
    """The Rosenbrock function"""
    a = 1.0
    b = 100.0
    ret = (a - x[0])**2 + b * (x[1] - x[0]**2)**2
    print(x, ret)
    return ret.astype(np.float32)


def rosenbrock_grad(x):
    """The gradient of the Rosenbrock function"""
    a = 1.0
    b = 100.0

    grad_x0 = 4 * b * x[0]**3 - 4 * b * x[0] * x[1] + 2 * x[0] - 2 * a

    grad_x1 = 2 * b * (x[1] - x[0]**2)

    # Return the gradient as a NumPy array
    return np.array([grad_x0, grad_x1], dtype=np.float32)


x0 = np.array([3.0, 21210.0], dtype=np.float32)

print(x0.dtype)
print(
    _optimize._minimize_bfgs(rosenbrock,
                             x0,
                             jac=rosenbrock_grad,
                             maxiter=100000,
                             gtol=1e-3))
```
